analysis.one_liner: Mandates annual oil and gas lease sales and fast-track permitting in Alaska's National Petroleum Reserve.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared committee on a 26-14 vote and sat on the House calendar from September 2013 without ever receiving a floor vote before that Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require the Interior Department to hold at least one oil and gas lease sale every year from 2013 through 2023 in the most commercially promising parts of the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska. It sets tight deadlines for approving roads and pipelines — permits for transport construction tied to existing leases would have to be approved within 60 days of the bill becoming law — and it throws out the management plan the Interior Department finalized in February 2013 and replaces it with one written to promote 'efficient and maximum development.' It also orders a full inventory of recoverable oil and gas, done with the state of Alaska and the American Association of Petroleum Geologists.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies that lease in the reserve. They would get guaranteed annual lease sales in the best acreage, hard deadlines that force the government to approve drilling and pipeline permits quickly, and federally planned road and pipeline rights-of-way designed so that every leasable tract is within 25 miles of infrastructure.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas lessees in Alaska

how_it_helps.text: Requires at least one competitive oil and gas lease sale each year, 2013 through 2023, in the areas of the reserve most likely to produce commercial quantities of oil and gas.

Requires federal agencies to approve permits for roads and pipelines serving existing leases within 60 days of enactment, and within 6 months for leases whose drilling-permit request has been submitted.
Directs Interior to submit a plan guaranteeing approved road and pipeline rights-of-way so that all leasable tracts in the reserve are within 25 miles of infrastructure.

Nullifies the February 21, 2013 Integrated Activity Plan and its environmental review, and requires a replacement plan and environmental impact statement written to promote efficient and maximum development of the reserve.

analysis.who_pays: The public. The reserve is federal land, so the land, the oil, and the environmental risk belong to everyone; this bill would trade management flexibility for a development mandate, would discard a completed environmental review, and would speed permitting of roads and pipelines across a large Arctic landscape where Alaska Native communities rely on subsistence hunting and fishing.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public and Alaska Native communities

drawbacks.text: The bill would void the February 2013 Record of Decision — the management plan Interior adopted after its own environmental review — and require its replacement with a plan aimed at maximum resource extraction, removing the balance that plan struck between leasing and protection of specific areas.

Mandatory annual lease sales and non-negotiable permitting deadlines (60 days for transport permits under existing leases, 60 days per permit under the new plan unless the applicant agrees to longer) substitute statutory clocks for site-by-site environmental judgment on roads, pipelines, and drilling across the reserve.

The resource assessment is to be carried out jointly with the American Association of Petroleum Geologists, an industry-affiliated professional society, alongside the U.S. Geological Survey and the state of Alaska, and the state may fund the federal assessment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the oil and gas industry the benefits are large and concrete: guaranteed annual sales of prime acreage, hard permit deadlines, and federally planned infrastructure access. The costs fall on the public side of the ledger: a congressionally mandated development program on federal land, the erasure of a finished management plan and environmental review, and shortened windows for environmental review of Arctic infrastructure. This is a one-directional bill — industry gains, and the public's main protection (a balanced, already-completed land-use plan) is what gets deleted.

outcome.mechanism: It passed committee on a 26-14 vote and was placed on the House calendar in September 2013, but the House never voted on it and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 14, 2013 by Rep. Doc Hastings with Rep. Don Young of Alaska as its only cosponsor.
It moved quickly in committee: a subcommittee hearing on May 22, subcommittee discharge and markup on June 12, and a 26-14 committee vote to order it reported.
It was reported without amendment on September 10, 2013 (H. Rept. 113-197) and placed on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 144, the step before floor consideration.
No further action appears in the record; the House never brought it to the floor and the Senate never considered it, and the bill expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public's existing protections held. The February 2013 management plan for the reserve stayed in force, oil companies did not get the mandated annual lease sales or the fast-track permitting deadlines, and no roads or pipelines were ordered planned under this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The 2013 land plan and its protections survived

sides.party_line_note: The only recorded vote was the 26-14 committee vote to report the bill, and the sources do not break that vote down by party; there was never a floor vote in either chamber.

industries.note: The bill would hand them guaranteed annual lease sales of the reserve's most promising acreage, hard permit deadlines, and federally planned road and pipeline access. Their gain comes from mandating extraction on public land and discarding the completed management plan that balanced development against other uses.

The bill requires Interior to plan rights-of-way so every leasable tract is within 25 miles of a road and pipeline, generating large construction projects on federal land. The profits ride on infrastructure whose environmental review deadlines the bill also shortens.

industries.industry: Alaska Native subsistence communities and conservation interests
industries.note: These interests supported the 2013 integrated activity plan, which the bill would nullify outright, and would bear the consequences of mandatory leasing, fast-tracked permitting, and mandated infrastructure across the reserve.
